Cork 2040: How Much Power, How Many Substations, What Budget?

Mankirat Singh · Portfolio · GitHub · LinkedIn

Co. Cork (Cork City and Cork County). Data: CSO metered electricity consumption and Census 2022 (heating, cars, population by electoral division); ESB Networks Demand Capacity Headroom Report and customer heatmap. 2040 is the year of ESB's Net Zero strategy. Independent analysis, not an ESB or ESB Networks publication.

Key findings

  • Co. Cork used 3,055 GWh of electricity in 2025, equivalent to a winter peak of about 581 MW.
  • By 2040 the peak could reach 1,110 MW in the central case (+91%), and 757–1,702 MW across scenarios. The biggest single driver is heat pumps, with about 128,536 extra heat pumps and 232,905 extra electric cars.
  • 45 of 65 Cork 110 kV / 38 kV substations would run short of capacity by 2040 (central case).
  • Meeting it needs about 10 new substations (10–90% range 5–16) plus about 45 upgrades, costing €194–346m in station investment alone (2026 prices).
  • Flexibility pays: smart EV charging, heat-pump flexibility and demand response cut the 2040 peak to 965 MW and the median station bill by about €68m (3 new stations instead of 10).
  • ESB Networks' own station forecasts point the same way: in 2040 Aggressive 33, Base 29, Best View 29, Conservative 26 Cork stations have no firm spare capacity left.

1. Where Cork starts

Yearly consumption is turned into a winter peak with a load factor of 0.60 (average ÷ peak), the quantity that sizes substations.

2. How much power Cork will need

The model adds, year by year: new homes and people, business growth, heat pumps (new homes plus conversions of oil-, gas- and solid-fuel-heated homes, mapped from Census 2022), electric cars (from Census car ownership), and new large loads, minus efficiency gains. Heat pumps and EVs follow an S-shaped uptake curve.

4. Which substations run out

Each electoral division's extra 2040 load is assigned to its nearest 110 kV or 38 kV station and compared with that station's spare capacity today (ESB Networks data). Only stations on ESB Networks' demand list take new load; generation-only stations such as wind farms and hydro are excluded. A small shortfall is met by upgrading the station (for example larger transformers); a larger one is met by upgrading it and adding new station(s) nearby for the rest.

How this compares: the central case here finds 45 stations short, closest to ESB Networks' Aggressive scenario (33). It is more demanding than all four, mainly because it assumes faster heat-pump and EV uptake to meet the 2040 net-zero path, and uses today's spare capacity from the heatmap rather than ESB Networks' planned reinforcements.

8. How Cork can accommodate it

  • Flexibility first. Smart EV charging and heat-pump flexibility are the cheapest "capacity": they defer or avoid stations (section 5). Time-of-use tariffs and managed charging should be in place before EV numbers peak.
  • Build where it runs out first. Stations that fill earliest (section 4) set the order of work; planning and consenting a 110 kV station takes years, so decisions are needed well before the year a station is full.
  • Upgrade before building. Where the shortfall is small, a larger transformer at an existing site is faster and cheaper than a new station.
  • Plan with the city. Growth is concentrated in Cork City and its expansion areas; reserving sites and cable routes in development plans now avoids costly retrofits later.
  • Keep the plan live. Re-run yearly as ESB Networks updates its workbooks and CSO publishes new data.

Limitations and methods

  • Consumption is metered energy by county; the winter peak is estimated with a load factor, not measured. Business and industry growth, new large loads, and EV charging behaviour are the least certain inputs.
  • Station assignment uses straight-line distance to the nearest station, a simplification of real network topology; ESB Networks' spare-capacity figures are indicative and can be limited by upstream circuits.
  • Costs cover stations only and use public examples and stated assumptions, not ESB Networks unit costs.
  • Methods: Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib). Bottom-up scenario model by electoral division with S-curve technology uptake; nearest-station spatial assignment; 5,000-run Monte Carlo over demand drivers, station sizes and unit costs (triangular distributions); one-at-a-time sensitivity; automatic reading of ESB Networks workbooks with structure detection and Irish Transverse Mercator conversion. Code: GitHub.
Data: CSO (CC BY 4.0); ESB Networks (DNDP). Analysis and any errors are the author's own.
